claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major players in many central biological processes.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major players in many central biological processes (Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008

claim: GPCRs likely explore complex conformational landscapes, characterized by several meta-stable structural states.
source: Indeed, GPCRs likely explore complex conformational landscapes, characterized by several meta-stable structural states.
evidence: Based on inference from the diversity in signaling properties and limitations of structural methods

claim: The relative distribution of GPCR conformational states is controlled by ligands, signaling proteins, and the environment, ultimately dictating the signaling output.
source: The relative distribution of these states is controlled by ligands, signaling proteins, and the environment, ultimately dictating the signaling output (Casiraghi et al., 2019; Hilger et al., 2018; Wingler and Lefkowitz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Many GPCR experimental structures indicate the occurrence of water molecules within their transmembrane (TM) regions.
source: Many GPCR experimental structures indicate the occurrence of water molecules within their transmembrane (TM) regions.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from GPCR structural studies

claim: Some water molecules are located in the ligand-binding pocket and directly contribute to the energetics of ligand binding.
source: Some are located in the ligand-binding pocket and directly contribute to the energetics of ligand binding (Deflorian et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deflorian et al., 2020

claim: Water molecules in different cavities have been proposed to be central to the allosteric propagation of conformational rearrangements required for receptor activation.
source: Others lie in different cavities and have been proposed to be central to the allosteric propagation of the conformational rearrangements required for receptor activation (Lesca et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The relationship between GPCR conformational dynamics and local hydration has been mostly inferred from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with rhodopsin and other receptors.
source: Indeed, the relationship between GPCR conformational dynamics and local hydration has been mostly inferred from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with rhodopsin (Grossfield et al., 2008) and other receptors as well (Yuan et al., 2014; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to MD simulation studies

claim: GHSR and its natural peptide agonist, ghrelin, are involved in most important biological processes such as the control of food intake, glucose metabolism, or reward and stress behaviors.
source: Indeed, this receptor and its natural peptide agonist, ghrelin, are involved in most important biological processes such as the control of food intake, glucose metabolism, or reward and stress behaviors (Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Müller et al., 2015

claim: L-(7-hydroxycoumarin-4-yl)-ethylglycine contains the L-(7-hydroxycoumarin-4-yl) (7H4MC) moiety whose emission properties are correlated to the presence of water molecules in its vicinity.
source: This UAA contains the L-(7-hydroxycoumarin-4-yl) (7H4MC) moiety whose emission properties are correlated to the presence of water molecules in its vicinity (Amaro et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amaro et al., 2015

claim: 7H4MC-ethylglycine was synthesized and introduced in GHSR using codon suppression technology.
source: 7H4MC-ethylglycine was synthesized as described in the Materials and methods section and introduced in GHSR using codon suppression technology (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2006 for codon suppression technology

claim: The labeled receptor was inserted into lipid nanodiscs formed by the scaffolding MSP1E3D1 protein and a POPC:POPG mixture.
source: To analyze receptor activation in a relevant membrane-like environment, the labeled receptor was inserted into lipid nanodiscs formed by the scaffolding MSP1E3D1 protein and a POPC:POPG mixture (see Materials and methods) (Damian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damian et al., 2012 and described in Materials and methods

claim: Homogeneous nanodisc populations of functional receptors were obtained.
source: Under such conditions, homogeneous nanodisc populations of functional receptors were obtained (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The active receptor was purified through a ligand affinity chromatography step to ensure all the receptors in the preparations were competent with regard to ligand binding.
source: Of importance, the active receptor was purified through a ligand affinity chromatography step to ensure all the receptors in our preparations were competent with regard to ligand binding (Ferré et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferré et al., 2019 and described methodology

claim: The receptor obtained under such conditions is totally functional with regard to ligand binding, and its pharmacological profile is closely related to that of GHSR expressed in HEK cell membranes.
source: Accordingly, we repeatedly demonstrated that the receptor obtained under such conditions is totally functional with regard to ligand binding, and that its pharmacological profile is closely related to that of GHSR expressed in HEK cell membranes (Ferré et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferré et al., 2019

claim: 7H4MC-ethylglycine was introduced at several single positions within the TM domains of GHSR: Y812.42, W1042.65, Y1062.67, F1193.28, F1213.30, I1343.43, F1794.61, W2155.41, Y2325.58, V2686.40, F2726.44, Y3037.33, or S3157.45.
source: 7H4MC-ethylglycine was introduced at several, single positions within the TM domains of GHSR, namely Y812.42, W1042.65, Y1062.67, F1193.28, F1213.30, I1343.43, F1794.61, W2155.41, Y2325.58, V2686.40, F2726.44, Y3037.33, or S3157.45 (superscript numbers follow Ballesteros-Weinstein numbering [Ballesteros and Weinstein, 1995; Figure 1A]).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Protein expression yields markedly decreased for all 7H4MC-ethylglycine mutants.
source: In all the cases, protein expression yields markedly decreased but, with the exception of the F1193.28 mutant that was not expressed at a detectable level, the amounts of purified receptor obtained were still compatible with the fluorescence experiments, that is, in the range of a hundred of µg per liter of bacterial culture.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the text

claim: The F1193.28 mutant was not expressed at a detectable level.
source: In all the cases, protein expression yields markedly decreased but, with the exception of the F1193.28 mutant that was not expressed at a detectable level, the amounts of purified receptor obtained were still compatible with the fluorescence experiments, that is, in the range of a hundred of µg per liter of bacterial culture.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the text

claim: Modified receptors bearing 7H4MC-ethylglycine at positions Y812.42, W1042.65, Y1062.67, F1193.28, F1213.30, F1794.61, and Y3037.43 could not be purified through the ligand affinity chromatography step.
source: However, the modified receptors bearing 7H4MC-ethylglycine at position Y812.42, W1042.65, Y1062.67, F1193.28, F1213.30, F1794.61, and Y3037.43 could not be purified through the ligand affinity chromatography step, indicating that replacing the native residue with 7H4MC-ethylglycine affected their three-dimensional fold and/or their ability to bind ligands.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the text

claim: Replacing the native residue with 7H4MC-ethylglycine at positions Y812.42, W1042.65, Y1062.67, F1193.28, F1213.30, F1794.61, and Y3037.43 affected the three-dimensional fold and/or ability to bind ligands.
source: However, the modified receptors bearing 7H4MC-ethylglycine at position Y812.42, W1042.65, Y1062.67, F1193.28, F1213.30, F1794.61, and Y3037.43 could not be purified through the ligand affinity chromatography step, indicating that replacing the native residue with 7H4MC-ethylglycine affected their three-dimensional fold and/or their ability to bind ligands.
evidence: Inferred from inability to purify through ligand affinity chromatography

claim: Replacing W2155.41 with 7H4MC-ethylglycine markedly decreased the basal activity of the receptor.
source: In addition, replacing W2155.41 with 7H4MC-ethylglycine markedly decreased the basal activity of the receptor, although this mutant could still bind its ligands and be activated by ghrelin.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the text

claim: The W2155.41 mutant could still bind its ligands and be activated by ghrelin.
source: In addition, replacing W2155.41 with 7H4MC-ethylglycine markedly decreased the basal activity of the receptor, although this mutant could still bind its ligands and be activated by ghrelin.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the text

claim: For positions I1343.43, Y2325.58, V2686.40, F2726.44, and S3157.45, replacing the naturally occurring residue with 7H4MC-ethylglycine affected neither ghrelin binding nor the receptor-catalyzed Gq activation in a relevant manner.
source: In contrast, for the other positions, that is, I1343.43, Y2325.58, V2686.40, F2726.44, and S3157.45, replacing the naturally occurring residue with 7H4MC-ethylglycine affected neither ghrelin binding nor the receptor-catalyzed Gq activation in a relevant manner (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B, C and supplementary figures

claim: The modified proteins displayed an emission spectrum characteristic of the 7H4MC moiety.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, the modified proteins displayed an emission spectrum characteristic of the 7H4MC moiety, while the wild-type receptor had no significant emission signal when excited at the same wavelength.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The wild-type receptor had no significant emission signal when excited at the same wavelength as the modified proteins.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, the modified proteins displayed an emission spectrum characteristic of the 7H4MC moiety, while the wild-type receptor had no significant emission signal when excited at the same wavelength.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The emission spectrum indicates an efficient incorporation of the labeled UAA into the receptor.
source: This indicates an efficient incorporation of the labeled UAA into the receptor.
evidence: Inferred from the characteristic emission spectrum of 7H4MC

claim: A difference in the H parameter inferred for the 7H4MC probe at the different positions of the apo GHSR was observed depending on the position considered.
source: A difference in the H parameter inferred for the 7H4MC probe at the different positions of the apo GHSR was observed depending on the position considered (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 2

claim: All positions were hydrated to some extent, but some displayed a high H value characteristic of high hydration whereas others displayed a low H value suggestive of a lower local hydration.
source: Indeed, all positions were hydrated to some extent, but some displayed a high H value characteristic of high hydration (3.43, 6.40) whereas others displayed a low H value suggestive of a lower local hydration (5.58, 6.44, 7.45).
evidence: Experimental observation from H parameter measurements

claim: 7H4MC fluorescence is a good indicator to discriminate between different local hydration states in the receptor structure.
source: This indicates that 7H4MC fluorescence is a good indicator to discriminate between different local hydration states in the receptor structure.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in H parameter at different positions

claim: Local hydration, as reported by 7H4MC fluorescence, depends on the region of the TM domain considered, with some regions more accessible to the solvent than others.
source: Besides, these data show that local hydration, as reported by 7H4MC fluorescence, depends on the region of the TM domain considered, with some regions more accessible to the solvent than others, even for closely related positions in the receptor structure (e.g., V2686.40 and F2726.44).
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in H parameter at different positions

claim: Binding of JMV3011 to labeled GHSR was not accompanied by a measurable change in the hydration parameter for any of the positions considered.
source: Binding of JMV3011 to labeled GHSR was not accompanied by a measurable change in the hydration parameter for any of the positions considered (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Binding of JMV3011 was not associated with any change in the conformation of isolated GHSR.
source: This is to be related to our previous observations demonstrating that binding of this compound was not associated with any change in the conformation of isolated GHSR (Mary et al., 2012; Damian et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Ghrelin binding was associated with an increase in the hydration parameter at position 5.58.
source: Specifically, ghrelin binding was associated with an increase in the hydration parameter at position 5.58 while local hydration at position 6.44 decreased (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, 5, 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4, 5, 6

claim: Ghrelin binding was associated with a decrease in local hydration at position 6.44.
source: Specifically, ghrelin binding was associated with an increase in the hydration parameter at position 5.58 while local hydration at position 6.44 decreased (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, 5, 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4, 5, 6

claim: No relevant change in the hydration parameter was observed for positions other than 5.58 and 6.44 upon ghrelin binding.
source: Besides 5.58 and 6.44, no relevant change in the hydration parameter was observed for the other positions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Agonist-induced GHSR activation is accompanied by a concerted parallel increase and decrease of the local hydration in specific regions of the receptor, namely TM5 and TM6.
source: This indicates that agonist-induced GHSR activation is accompanied by a concerted parallel increase and decrease of the local hydration in specific regions of the receptor, namely here TM5 and TM6.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in H parameter at positions 5.58 and 6.44

claim: 7H4MC fluorescence is well adapted to monitor hydration changes in a very local environment.
source: This suggests that 7H4MC fluorescence is well adapted to monitor hydration changes in a very local environment and that changes in local hydration likely occur at specific, spatially restricted sites.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that V2686.40 and F2726.44 show different hydration changes despite being close in structure

claim: Changes in local hydration likely occur at specific, spatially restricted sites.
source: This suggests that 7H4MC fluorescence is well adapted to monitor hydration changes in a very local environment and that changes in local hydration likely occur at specific, spatially restricted sites.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that V2686.40 and F2726.44 show different hydration changes despite being close in structure

claim: Binding of the inverse agonist SPA was accompanied by a change in the hydration parameter opposite to that observed with ghrelin.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, binding of the inverse agonist SPA was accompanied by a change in the hydration parameter opposite to that observed with ghrelin, that is, the H parameter decreased and increased for positions 5.58 and 6.44, respectively (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), consistent with the opposite effect of ghrelin and SPA on GHSR activation and conformational landscape (Mary et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, and citation to Mary et al., 2012

claim: The H parameter decreased at position 5.58 and increased at position 6.44 upon SPA binding.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, binding of the inverse agonist SPA was accompanied by a change in the hydration parameter opposite to that observed with ghrelin, that is, the H parameter decreased and increased for positions 5.58 and 6.44, respectively (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), consistent with the opposite effect of ghrelin and SPA on GHSR activation and conformational landscape (Mary et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The hydration pattern in the presence of JMV3002 was different from that observed in the presence of ghrelin.
source: Finally, the hydration pattern in the presence of JMV3002 was different from that observed in the presence of ghrelin.
evidence: Experimental observation from H parameter measurements

claim: Binding of JMV3002 was accompanied by a decrease in the hydration parameter at position 6.44.
source: Indeed, while the binding of this compound was still accompanied by a decrease in the hydration parameter at position 6.44, as in the case of ghrelin binding, no change was observed for the probe at position 5.58 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: No change in the hydration parameter was observed for position 5.58 upon JMV3002 binding.
source: Indeed, while the binding of this compound was still accompanied by a decrease in the hydration parameter at position 6.44, as in the case of ghrelin binding, no change was observed for the probe at position 5.58 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The difference in hydration pattern between ghrelin and JMV3002 could be related to the differences in their pharmacological profiles.
source: This could be related to the differences in the pharmacological profile of the two compounds, as ghrelin is a full agonist whereas JMV3002 is a Gq partial agonist that triggers neither Gi activation nor arrestin recruitment (M'Kadmi et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in hydration pattern and supported by citation to M'Kadmi et al., 2015

claim: Ghrelin is a full agonist.
source: This could be related to the differences in the pharmacological profile of the two compounds, as ghrelin is a full agonist whereas JMV3002 is a Gq partial agonist that triggers neither Gi activation nor arrestin recruitment (M'Kadmi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to M'Kadmi et al., 2015

claim: JMV3002 is a Gq partial agonist that triggers neither Gi activation nor arrestin recruitment.
source: This could be related to the differences in the pharmacological profile of the two compounds, as ghrelin is a full agonist whereas JMV3002 is a Gq partial agonist that triggers neither Gi activation nor arrestin recruitment (M'Kadmi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to M'Kadmi et al., 2015

claim: Five MD simulations of 5 µs were run for each conformational state of the receptor, totalizing 50 µs of all-atoms simulation.
source: To provide a structural framework to our experimental observations and observe possible differences between the hydration pattern of inactive and active-like conformers of wild-type GHSR, we then ran five MD simulations of 5 µs for each conformational state of the receptor, totalizing 50 µs of all-atoms simulation.
evidence: Described methodology in the text

claim: The crystal structure of the inactive, antagonist-loaded state of the receptor has been solved.
source: The crystal structure of the inactive, antagonist-loaded state of the receptor has been solved (Shiimura et al., 2020) and was used as a starting point for our MD studies.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shiimura et al., 2020

claim: Two cryo-EM structures of the ghrelin receptor in complex with ghrelin or a synthetic agonist and a Gq mimetic have been posted on the BioRxiv preprint server.
source: Besides, two cryo-EM structures of the ghrelin receptor in complex with ghrelin or a synthetic agonist and a Gq mimetic have been posted on the BioRxiv preprint server (https://doi.org/10.1101/2021.06.09.447478).
evidence: Reference to preprint server

claim: The coordinates of the cryo-EM structures are not yet available.
source: However, since the coordinates of these structures are not yet available, we had to model an active-like state of GHSR in the absence of its cognate G protein (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statement of fact about availability of structural data

claim: An active-like state of GHSR in the absence of its cognate G protein was modeled.
source: However, since the coordinates of these structures are not yet available, we had to model an active-like state of GHSR in the absence of its cognate G protein (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Described methodology in the text

claim: A projection of all conformers explored during the simulations confirmed their compatibility with experimental structures, describing mainly inactive and intermediate states.
source: A projection of all conformers explored during our simulations confirmed their compatibility with experimental structures, describing mainly inactive and intermediate states (based on the classification in the GPCRdb; Pándy-Szekeres et al., 2018), the latter corresponding to an activated receptor without the G protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Pándy-Szekeres et al., 2018

claim: Intermediate states correspond to an activated receptor without the G protein.
source: A projection of all conformers explored during our simulations confirmed their compatibility with experimental structures, describing mainly inactive and intermediate states (based on the classification in the GPCRdb; Pándy-Szekeres et al., 2018), the latter corresponding to an activated receptor without the G protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on classification in the GPCRdb, supported by citation to Pándy-Szekeres et al., 2018

claim: Analysis of the statistical water distribution in GHSR confirmed that differences in the hydration pattern could exist depending on its inactive/active states.
source: Interestingly, analysis of the statistical water distribution in GHSR confirmed that differences in the hydration pattern could exist depending on its inactive/active states (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: These differences in hydration pattern effectively occurred in the regions where the 7H4MC-ethylglycine residue had been inserted in the experiments.
source: More importantly, these differences effectively occurred in the regions where the 7H4MC-ethylglycine residue had been inserted in our experiments.
evidence: Comparison of MD simulation results with experimental design

claim: Four out of five simulations starting from the X-ray (inactive) structure of GHSR converged toward a same hydration pattern.
source: Four out of five simulations starting from the X-ray (inactive) structure of GHSR converged toward a same hydration pattern (Figure 3A-D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A-D

claim: In the fifth simulation starting from the inactive structure, the water statistically occupied a larger volume on the intracellular side of the receptor.
source: In the last simulation (Figure 3E), the water statistically occupied a larger volume on the intracellular side of the receptor.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The distribution of water molecules in the inactive state was in agreement with the distribution described recently for other receptors of the same family using similar methods.
source: Of interest, this distribution of water molecules in the inactive state was in agreement with the distribution described recently for other receptors of the same family using similar methods (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019; Bertalan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019 and Bertalan et al., 2020

claim: In agreement with experimental data, the water distribution in the inactive conformation of the receptor showed the presence of water molecules around F2726.44 whereas Y2325.58 was not solvated.
source: In agreement with our experimental data, the water distribution in the inactive conformation of the receptor showed the presence of water molecules around F2726.44 whereas Y2325.58 was not solvated.
evidence: Comparison of MD simulation results with experimental data

claim: I1343.43 was in contact with water molecules in the inactive conformation.
source: Accordingly, I1343.43 was also in contact with water molecules.

claim: V2686.40 was not in contact with water molecule in the inactive state whereas S3157.45 was, in contradiction with experimental data.
source: However, and in contradiction with our experiments, V2686.40 was not in contact with water molecule in the inactive state whereas S3157.45 was.
evidence: Comparison of MD simulation results with experimental data

claim: V2686.40 occupies a central position in the receptor whereas S3157.45 is close to the interface between TM6 and TM7.
source: V2686.40 occupies a central position in the receptor whereas S3157.45 is close to the interface between TM6 and TM7 (Figure 4).
evidence: Structural observation shown in Figure 4

claim: Insertion of 7H4MC-ethylglycine at positions 1343.43, 2325.58, and 2726.44 are more conservative in terms of residue size.
source: If insertion of 7H4MC-ethylglycine at positions 1343.43, 2325.58, and 2726.44 are more conservative in terms of residue size, the insertion of 7H4MC in place of a valine (V2686.40) or a serine (S3157.45) suggests a stronger adaptation of the receptor fold to these mutations.
evidence: Inference based on residue size comparison

claim: The insertion of 7H4MC in place of a valine (V2686.40) or a serine (S3157.45) suggests a stronger adaptation of the receptor fold to these mutations.
source: If insertion of 7H4MC-ethylglycine at positions 1343.43, 2325.58, and 2726.44 are more conservative in terms of residue size, the insertion of 7H4MC in place of a valine (V2686.40) or a serine (S3157.45) suggests a stronger adaptation of the receptor fold to these mutations.
evidence: Inference based on residue size comparison

claim: Adiabatic maps were computed for positions 2686.40 and 3157.45.
source: To clarify the possible orientations of 7H4MC-ethylglycine into the receptor, we thus computed adiabatic maps for positions 2686.40 and 3157.45 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Described methodology and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The adiabatic map confirmed that 7H4MC-ethylglycine at position 2686.40 allowed interaction with solvent molecules.
source: In the case of 7H4MC-ethylglycine at position 2686.40, the adiabatic map confirmed that this large residue, in comparison to a valine, allowed interaction with solvent molecules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: For the 3157.45 position, the adiabatic map suggested that this residue could conserve its initial orientation toward the interior of the receptor and should be highly solvated.
source: For the 3157.45 position, even the adiabatic map suggested that this residue could conserve its initial orientation toward the interior of the receptor and should be highly solvated.
evidence: Inference from adiabatic map analysis

claim: A different hydration pattern was found in the fifth simulation starting from the inactive state.
source: Interestingly, a different hydration pattern was found in the fifth simulation.
evidence: MD simulation result

claim: The different hydration pattern in the fifth simulation was explained by a spreading of TM6 during the simulation.
source: This profile was explained by a spreading of TM6 during the simulation, thus leading to conformers close to those observed when starting from the active-like state (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The resulting hydration pattern in the fifth simulation was very close to that obtained in the simulations starting from the active-like state.
source: Accordingly, the resulting hydration pattern was very close to that obtained in the simulations starting from the active-like state (Figure 3F-I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3F-I

claim: In the active-like hydration pattern, water molecules were more uniformly distributed in the receptor including its lower, intracellular part.
source: In this pattern, water molecules were more uniformly distributed in the receptor including its lower, intracellular part.
evidence: MD simulation result

claim: The main structural difference between inactive and active states was the spreading of TM6.
source: Indeed, the main structural difference between both states was the spreading of TM6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which contributed to a large water influx into the intracellular moiety of the receptor.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The spreading of TM6 contributed to a large water influx into the intracellular moiety of the receptor.
source: Indeed, the main structural difference between both states was the spreading of TM6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which contributed to a large water influx into the intracellular moiety of the receptor.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: In the active-like pattern, I1343.43, Y2326.44, and V2686.40 were all in close contact with water molecules.
source: In this pattern, and in agreement with the fluorescence experiments, I1343.43, Y2326.44, and V2686.40 were all in close contact with water molecules whereas F2726.44 was flipped toward TM5, contributing to reduce its interactions with surrounding water (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: In the active-like pattern, F2726.44 was flipped toward TM5, contributing to reduce its interactions with surrounding water.
source: In this pattern, and in agreement with the fluorescence experiments, I1343.43, Y2326.44, and V2686.40 were all in close contact with water molecules whereas F2726.44 was flipped toward TM5, contributing to reduce its interactions with surrounding water (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: The structural feature of F2726.44 flipping toward TM5 was found to be conserved in all GPCRs.
source: This structural feature was found to be conserved in all GPCRs (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: A simulation starting from the active state showed a closure and a loss of hydration in the intracellular part of the receptor due to a motion of TM7 inside the receptor.
source: We also obtained a simulation starting from the active state that showed a different behavior from other simulations, that is, a closure and a loss of hydration in the intracellular part of the receptor due to a motion of TM7 inside the receptor (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3J

claim: The motion of TM7 inside the receptor was compatible with the direction coded by the experimental structures and shown by principal component analysis (PCA).
source: Such a motion was compatible with the direction coded by the experimental structures and shown by principal component analysis (PCA), where the first two eigenvectors displayed this inward motion of TM7 concomitant to TM6 spreading (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: The first two eigenvectors from PCA displayed an inward motion of TM7 concomitant to TM6 spreading.
source: Such a motion was compatible with the direction coded by the experimental structures and shown by principal component analysis (PCA), where the first two eigenvectors displayed this inward motion of TM7 concomitant to TM6 spreading (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: In the simulation with TM7 motion, the resulting hydration pattern was very close to those observed in the simulations starting from the inactive state.
source: Accordingly, in this simulation, the resulting hydration pattern was very close to those observed in the simulations starting from the inactive state (Figure 3A-D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A-D

claim: The H parameter for positions 5.58 and 6.44 was measured with GHSR assembled into POPC:POPG nanodiscs in the absence or presence of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: Specifically, we measured the hydration parameter for the probe at positions 5.58 and 6.44 with GHSR assembled into POPC:POPG nanodiscs in the absence or presence of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), a lipid that has been shown to impact on the activity of many different membrane proteins (Hammond and Burke, 2020) including GPCRs (Yen et al., 2018) and, more recently, the ghrelin receptor (Damian et al., 2021).

claim: PIP2 has been shown to impact on the activity of many different membrane proteins including GPCRs.
source: Specifically, we measured the hydration parameter for the probe at positions 5.58 and 6.44 with GHSR assembled into POPC:POPG nanodiscs in the absence or presence of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), a lipid that has been shown to impact on the activity of many different membrane proteins (Hammond and Burke, 2020) including GPCRs (Yen et al., 2018) and, more recently, the ghrelin receptor (Damian et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammond and Burke, 2020; Yen et al., 2018; and Damian et al., 2021

claim: The H parameter for the two positions that were sensitive to receptor activation was further affected by PIP2.
source: As shown in Figure 5, the H parameter for the two positions that were sensitive to receptor activation was further affected by PIP2.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5

claim: Adding 2.5% of PIP2 to the nanodiscs increased the H parameter for position 5.58 and concomitantly decreased that for position 6.44.
source: Indeed, adding 2.5% of this lipid to the nanodiscs increased the H parameter for position 5.58 and concomitantly decreased that for position 6.44.
evidence: Experimental observation from H parameter measurements

claim: PIP2 exalted the effect of the full agonist ghrelin on the receptor hydration features.
source: PIP2 therefore exalted the effect of the full agonist ghrelin had on the receptor hydration features.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in H parameter with PIP2

claim: PIP2 further shifts the conformational equilibrium toward hydration pattern associated with the active-like conformation of GHSR.
source: This suggests that PIP2 further shifts the conformational equilibrium toward hydration pattern associated with the active-like conformation of GHSR, indicative of an allosteric coupling between the full agonist and PIP2 for stabilizing this state.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in H parameter with PIP2

claim: There is an allosteric coupling between the full agonist and PIP2 for stabilizing the active-like state of GHSR.
source: This suggests that PIP2 further shifts the conformational equilibrium toward hydration pattern associated with the active-like conformation of GHSR, indicative of an allosteric coupling between the full agonist and PIP2 for stabilizing this state.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in H parameter with PIP2

claim: The effect of PIP2 on hydration pattern could explain the impact of PIP2 on GHSR-catalyzed G protein activation.
source: This effect could explain the impact of PIP2 on GHSR-catalyzed G protein activation (Damian et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in H parameter with PIP2 and supported by citation to Damian et al., 2021

claim: Local hydration and polar networks have been proposed to play a role in the allosteric activation process of GPCRs.
source: Local hydration and polar networks have been proposed to play a role in the allosteric activation process of GPCRs, as it is the case for many other proteins (Leitner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leitner et al., 2020

claim: 7H4MC-ethylglycine includes the 7H4MC fluorophore whose emission properties are directly dependent on the water content in its microenvironment.
source: Specifically, 7H4MC-ethylglycine was incorporated at specific positions in GHSR through codon suppression technology. 7H4MC-ethylglycine includes the 7H4MC fluorophore whose emission properties are directly dependent on the water content in its microenvironment (Georgieva et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Georgieva et al., 2005

claim: The 7H4MC chromophore has been shown not to affect the global hydration levels but, in some particular situations, only to influence the residence time of water molecules.
source: Of importance, this chromophore has been shown not to affect the global hydration levels but, in some particular situations, only to influence the residence time of water molecules (Georgieva et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Georgieva et al., 2005

claim: The 7H4MC chromophore should not markedly modify the hydration pattern of the protein, with the condition it does not affect its three-dimensional fold.
source: It therefore should not markedly modify the hydration pattern of the protein, with the condition it does not affect its three-dimensional fold (Georgieva et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Georgieva et al., 2005

claim: Incorporation of 7H4MC-ethylglycine at positions I1343.43, Y2325.58, V2686.40, F2726.44, and S3157.45 does not dramatically perturb the three-dimensional fold of the ghrelin receptor.
source: This suggests that incorporation of 7H4MC-ethylglycine at these positions does not dramatically perturb the three-dimensional fold of the ghrelin receptor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that these mutants did not affect ghrelin binding or Gq activation

claim: Mutating F2726.44 to an alanine had been shown to abolish GHSR constitutive activity and reduce ghrelin-induced signaling without affecting ghrelin binding affinity.
source: The absence of major effect on substituting F2726.44 with 7H4MC-ethylglycine on GHSR functioning was puzzling, as mutating this residue to an alanine had been shown to abolish GHSR constitutive activity and reduce ghrelin-induced signaling without affecting ghrelin binding affinity (Valentin-Hansen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valentin-Hansen et al., 2012

claim: Replacing F2726.44 with a tyrosine had a far lower impact on both basal- and ghrelin-induced GHSR activity.
source: However, replacing the phenylalanine with a tyrosine had a far lower impact on both basal- and ghrelin-induced GHSR activity (Valentin-Hansen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valentin-Hansen et al., 2012

claim: A rigid, aromatic group is required at position F2726.44 for stabilizing the receptor active state.
source: As concluded by the authors, a possible mechanism would be that a rigid, aromatic group is required at this position for stabilizing the receptor active state.
evidence: Inference from previous study, supported by citation to Valentin-Hansen et al., 2012

claim: The requirement for a rigid, aromatic group at position F2726.44 could explain why replacing phenylalanine with 7H4MC-ethylglycine did not lead to a major decrease in GHSR activity.
source: This could explain why replacing phenylalanine with 7H4MC-ethylglycine did not lead to a major decrease in GHSR activity.
evidence: Inference from the observation that 7H4MC-ethylglycine contains an aromatic group

claim: The fluorescence properties of 7H4MC were affected by the activation state of GHSR only when the probe was located at positions 5.58 and 6.44.
source: The fluorescence properties of 7H4MC were affected by the activation state of GHSR only when the probe was located at positions 5.58 and 6.44.
evidence: Experimental observation from fluorescence measurements

claim: Highly hydrated, invariant positions were observed besides positions 5.58 and 6.44.
source: Besides these two positions, highly hydrated, invariant positions were observed.
evidence: Experimental observation from fluorescence measurements

claim: Highly hydrated, invariant positions could correspond to regions of the receptor directly accessible to the solvent whatever its activation state is.
source: These could correspond to regions of the receptor directly accessible to the solvent whatever its activation state is.
evidence: Speculation about the nature of invariant hydrated positions

claim: Hydration at invariant positions could include the contribution of water molecules with a structural rather than a functional role.
source: Alternatively, hydration at these positions could include the contribution of water molecules with a structural rather than a functional role.
evidence: Speculation about the nature of invariant hydrated positions

claim: Changes in the hydration pattern of GPCRs have been shown either to involve a direct rearrangement of the water molecules in the receptor ligand-binding pocket upon ligand binding or to result from the conformational changes associated with receptor activation.
source: Changes in the hydration pattern of GPCRs have been shown either to involve a direct rearrangement of the water molecules in the receptor ligand-binding pocket upon ligand binding or to result from the conformational changes associated with receptor activation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from GPCR studies

claim: Positions Y2325.58 and F2726.44 are both located outside the major putative ligand-binding pocket of GHSR.
source: The two positions where we observed a change in the H parameter upon agonist binding, that is, Y2325.58 and F2726.44, are both located outside the major putative ligand-binding pocket of GHSR (Shiimura et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shiimura et al., 2020

claim: The effects observed on the H parameter upon ligand binding are not likely to be the direct consequence of the rearrangement of water molecules within the GHSR binding pocket.
source: The effects we observed on the H parameter upon ligand binding are thus not likely to be the direct consequence of the rearrangement of water molecules within the GHSR binding pocket but may rather result from differences in the hydration pattern of the different conformational states of GHSR, as fully supported by our MD simulations.
evidence: Inferred from the location of positions 5.58 and 6.44 outside the binding pocket

claim: The effects observed on the H parameter upon ligand binding may result from differences in the hydration pattern of the different conformational states of GHSR.
source: The effects we observed on the H parameter upon ligand binding are thus not likely to be the direct consequence of the rearrangement of water molecules within the GHSR binding pocket but may rather result from differences in the hydration pattern of the different conformational states of GHSR, as fully supported by our MD simulations.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation results

claim: The emission profile of 7H4MC reflects the average, equilibrium contribution of the hydration pattern in the different GHSR states present in the solution.
source: The emission profile of 7H4MC reflects the average, equilibrium contribution of the hydration pattern in the different GHSR states present in the solution.
evidence: Based on understanding of fluorescence spectroscopy

claim: Any change in the emission properties of the 7H4MC probe implies a change in the distribution of the different states in the receptor conformational landscape and a difference in the hydration features of these states.
source: Any change in the emission properties of the probe thus implies (i) a change in the distribution of the different states in the receptor conformational landscape and (ii) a difference in the hydration features of these states.
evidence: Logical inference from the nature of the fluorescence measurement

claim: The remodeling of the hydration pattern is an integral component of the rearrangement of the GHSR conformational repertoire associated with receptor activation.
source: Taken together, the variations we observed therefore demonstrate that the remodeling of the hydration pattern is an integral component of the rearrangement of the GHSR conformational repertoire associated with receptor activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in H parameter upon ligand binding

claim: The remodeling of hydration pattern is directly correlated to concerted, specific and well-defined movements in the TM domains of the receptor.
source: This remodeling is directly correlated to concerted, specific and well-defined movements in the TM domains of the receptor, as demonstrated by MD.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation results

claim: The findings are fully consistent with previous work demonstrating the role of water molecules in the activation process of other GPCRs such as the GLP-1 receptor.
source: This is fully consistent with previous work demonstrating the role of water molecules in the activation process of other GPCRs such as the GLP-1 receptor (Zhao et al., 2020; Wootten et al., 2016a; Wootten et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on GLP-1 receptor

claim: Whether the data reflects that water molecules are allosteric players in the activation process or that the movements of water molecules compensate the changes in the intramolecular voids within the different states involved in receptor activation remains an open question.
source: Whether our data reflects the fact that water molecules are allosteric players in the activation process, as demonstrated for other proteins including rhodopsin (Chawla et al., 2021), or that the movements of water molecules compensate the changes in the intramolecular voids within the different states involved in receptor activation remains an open question.
evidence: Speculation about the interpretation of the results, with citation to Chawla et al., 2021

claim: MD simulations were used to provide a structural framework to the experimental observables.
source: In parallel to the fluorescence approach, we used a complementary approach based on MD simulations that was aimed at providing a structural framework to the experimental observables.
evidence: Described methodology in the text

claim: The MD method is dedicated to the exploration of the conformational space accessible to the receptor without any bias.
source: This method is dedicated to the exploration of the conformational space accessible to the receptor without any bias.
evidence: Description of the MD methodology

claim: Structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) can help in identifying hotspots for protein-water interactions, but in more than half of the available structures the resolution is not good enough to observe any water molecules.
source: Indeed, structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) can help in identifying hotspots for protein-water interactions, but in more than half of the available structures the resolution is not good enough to observe any water molecules.
evidence: Based on knowledge of PDB structures

claim: Static structures do not inform about the dynamical behavior of water molecule inside the receptor.
source: Moreover, static structures do not inform about the dynamical behavior of water molecule inside the receptor.
evidence: Based on understanding of structural methods

claim: MD simulations of inactive and active state of GHSR allowed analysis of a fully solvated receptor, where the global hydration pattern varied as a function of the conformational state of the receptor.
source: MD simulations of inactive and active state of GHSR allowed us to analyze a fully solvated receptor, where the global hydration pattern varied as a function of the conformational state of the receptor.
evidence: Description of MD simulation results

claim: Sidechain positions and hydration patterns in both states were compatible with the experiment for positions 1343.43, 2325.58, 2686.40, and 2726.44.
source: Even though we simulated the wild-type GHSR, sidechain positions and hydration patterns in both states were compatible with our experiment for positions 1343.43, 2325.58, 2686.40, and 2726.44.
evidence: Comparison of MD simulation results with experimental data

claim: The hydration at position 3157.45 did not agree with experimental results.
source: In contrast, however, the hydration at position 3157.45 did not agree with our experimental results.
evidence: Comparison of MD simulation results with experimental data

claim: A possibility for the disagreement at position 3157.45 would be that the size of the residue itself excludes water molecules from its vicinity, and/or orients it toward the membrane.
source: A possibility would be that the size of the residue itself excludes water molecules from its vicinity, and/or orients it toward the membrane, thus explaining the low hydration in the inactive and the active states of the receptor we measured experimentally.
evidence: Speculation about the reason for disagreement between MD and experiment

claim: A difference in the GHSR hydration pattern was observed depending on whether the ligand was a full or a Gq-biased agonist.
source: Interestingly, a difference in the GHSR hydration pattern was observed depending on whether the ligand was a full or a Gq-biased agonist.
evidence: Experimental observation from H parameter measurements

claim: The difference in hydration pattern indicates a different arrangement of the water network in the conformational states stabilized by full and Gq-biased agonists.
source: This indicates a different arrangement of the water network in the conformational states stabilized by these ligands.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in hydration pattern

claim: Mutation of the water hydrogen bond network in NK1R affected Gq- and Gs-mediated signaling in a different way.
source: This is in line with previous observations with NK1R where mutation of the water hydrogen bond network affected Gq- and Gs-mediated signaling in a different way (Valentin-Hansen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valentin-Hansen et al., 2015

claim: The central polar network in the GLP1 receptor has been suggested to be critical for G protein-dependent but not for G protein-independent signaling.
source: In the same way, the central polar network in the GLP1 receptor has been suggested to be critical for G protein-dependent but not for G protein-independent signaling (Wootten et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wootten et al., 2016a

claim: The different states in the GHSR conformational landscape differ in their hydration pattern.
source: Taken together, this data indicates that the different states in the GHSR conformational landscape differ in their hydration pattern, as stated above but, in addition, that ligands with different pharmacological profiles, here a full and a partial, biased agonist, have a different impact on the distribution of these states.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in hydration pattern with different ligands

claim: Ligands with different pharmacological profiles have a different impact on the distribution of conformational states.
source: Taken together, this data indicates that the different states in the GHSR conformational landscape differ in their hydration pattern, as stated above but, in addition, that ligands with different pharmacological profiles, here a full and a partial, biased agonist, have a different impact on the distribution of these states.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in hydration pattern with different ligands

claim: The conclusion with GHSR is consistent with previous data using a different conformational reporter, monobromobimane.
source: This conclusion with GHSR is consistent with our previous data using a different conformational reporter, monobromobimane (Mary et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mary et al., 2012

claim: The lipid bilayer composition has been shown to impact on the structure and function of many different membrane proteins including ion channels and receptors.
source: This is the case of the lipid bilayer whose composition has been shown to impact on the structure and function of many different membrane proteins including ion channels (Hille et al., 2015) and receptors (Strohman et al., 2019; Dawaliby et al., 2016; Casiraghi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: PIP2 has been shown to stabilize the receptor:G protein complex for the adenosine A2a-, β1-adrenergic, and neurotensin receptor 1.
source: Among the lipids reported to affect GPCR signaling such as cholesterol (Casiraghi et al., 2016; Zocher et al., 2012) or charged phospholipids (Strohman et al., 2019; Dawaliby et al., 2016), PIP2 has been shown to stabilize the receptor:G protein complex for the adenosine A2a-, β1-adrenergic, and neurotensin receptor 1 (Yen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yen et al., 2018

claim: PIP2 could be an allosteric regulator of ghrelin signaling.
source: More recently, we showed that PIP2 could be an allosteric regulator of ghrelin signaling (Damian et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damian et al., 2021

claim: Including PIP2 in the nanodiscs was associated with a further amplification of the changes in 7H4MC fluorescence triggered by ghrelin.
source: Accordingly, we observed here that including PIP2 in the nanodiscs was associated with a further amplification of the changes in 7H4MC fluorescence triggered by ghrelin, reflecting the allosteric coupling between the full agonist and this lipid for stabilizing an active-like hydration pattern of GHSR.
evidence: Experimental observation from fluorescence measurements

claim: The combination of incorporation of 7H4MC-ethylglycine into proteins, fluorescence spectroscopy, and advanced MD simulations provided a straightforward strategy to delineate conformational events associated with GHSR activation through local hydration.
source: In closing, the combination of incorporation of 7H4MC-ethylglycine into proteins, fluorescence spectroscopy, and advanced MD simulations provided us with a straightforward strategy to delineate conformational events associated with GHSR activation through an unexplored but nevertheless central feature in the functioning of membrane proteins, local hydration.
evidence: Summary of the methodological approach and its utility

claim: The hydration pattern in specific regions of TM5 and TM6 is dependent on the activation state of the receptor.
source: Using this strategy, we found that the hydration pattern in specific regions of TM5 and TM6 is dependent on the activation state of the receptor.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The findings illuminate an unexpected role of water molecules as possible allosteric modulators of GHSR activation.
source: This illuminates an unexpected role of water molecules as possible allosteric modulators of GHSR activation, consistent with their general effect on the allosteric regulation of proteins (Leitner et al., 2020).
evidence: Interpretation of findings, supported by citation to Leitner et al., 2020

claim: A model emerges where the activation process of GPCRs and their final signaling output could be the result of the concerted, synergistic, and exquisitely tuned influence of all the components in the receptor environment, including the solvent, on the distribution of the different states composing their conformational landscape.
source: Hence, a model emerges where the activation process of GPCRs and their final signaling output could be the result of the concerted, synergistic, and exquisitely tuned influence of all the components in the receptor environment, including the solvent, on the distribution of the different states composing their conformational landscape.
evidence: Proposed model based on the findings

claim: Water movements are tightly correlated to the receptor activation process and could be used as a fingerprint to navigate the conformational landscape of GPCRs.
source: In addition, these observations demonstrate that water movements are tightly correlated to the receptor activation process and could therefore be used as a fingerprint to navigate the conformational landscape of GPCRs.
evidence: Interpretation of findings and proposed application

claim: The conformational dynamics of GHSR are tightly coupled to the movements of internal water molecules.
source: These results demonstrate that the conformational dynamics of GHSR are tightly coupled to the movements of internal water molecules, further enhancing our understanding of the molecular bases of GPCR-mediated signaling.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study

claim: GHSR is characterized by a specific hydration pattern that is selectively remodeled by pharmacologically distinct ligands and by the lipid environment.
source: We found that GHSR is characterized by a specific hydration pattern that is selectively remodeled by pharmacologically distinct ligands and by the lipid environment.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study

claim: The remodeling of GHSR hydration pattern is directly related to the concerted movements of the transmembrane domains of the receptor.
source: This process is directly related to the concerted movements of the transmembrane domains of the receptor.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study
